summary.text: For \(n=550172=4\cdot343\cdot401\), congruence periodicity forces any occurrence of residue \(63945\) into 200 arithmetic progressions of period \(80200\); a finite modular check shows none occurs before \(16331504\), while a separate finite computation shows every residue is covered by \(17135927\). A prime-counting computation gives \(p_{550172}\le8165753\), hence \(2(p_{550172}-1)\le16331504\le a(550172)\), contradicting the strict inequality.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 f(k)=2^k-k
\]
and, for a positive integer \(n\), let \(a(n)\) be the least positive integer \(m\) such that the residues of \(f(1),\ldots,f(m)\) modulo \(n\) include every residue class modulo \(n\).

We disprove the conjectured inequality by taking
\[
 N=550172.
\]
The relevant numerical constants are
\[
 R=63945,\qquad B=16331504,\qquad C=17135927,
\]
and
\[
 P=8165753.
\]
We will prove
\[
 a(N)\ge B
\]
and
\[
 p_N=P,
\]
where \(p_N\) is the \(N\)-th prime. Since
\[
 2(P-1)=2(8165753-1)=16331504=B,
\]
these statements give
\[
 a(N)\ge 2(p_N-1),
\]
which directly contradicts the strict inequality asserted in the conjecture. We will also establish that all residues are covered by time \(C\), so that the minimum defining \(a(N)\) is certainly attained.

Throughout, congruences involving \(2^k-k\) may be manipulated as ordinary integer congruences. There is no issue from viewing the expression as a natural-number subtraction, because
\[
 k\le 2^k\qquad(k\ge0).
\]
For example, this follows by induction: it is immediate for \(k=0,1\), and if \(k+1\le2^{k+1}\), then
\[
 k+2\le2(k+1)\le2^{k+2}.
\]

## 1. Restricting all possible occurrences of the residue \(R\)

The factorization of the chosen modulus is
\[
 N=550172=4\cdot343\cdot401=4\cdot7^3\cdot401.
\]
In particular, \(401\mid N\), and
\[
 R=63945\equiv186\pmod{401}.
\]
Also, direct repeated squaring gives
\[
 2^{200}\equiv1\pmod{401}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
 2^k\equiv2^{k\bmod200}\pmod{401}
\]
for every \(k\).

Suppose that an exponent \(k\) hits the selected residue modulo \(N\), that is,
\[
 2^k-k\equiv R\pmod N. \tag{1}
\]
Reducing (1) modulo \(401\) yields
\[
 2^k-k\equiv186\pmod{401},
\]
or equivalently
\[
 2^k\equiv186+k\pmod{401}. \tag{2}
\]
Write
\[
 k=200q+i,\qquad 0\le i<200.
\]
Using \(2^{200}\equiv1\pmod{401}\), equation (2) becomes
\[
 2^i\equiv186+200q+i\pmod{401}.
\]
Thus
\[
 200q\equiv2^i-186-i\pmod{401}. \tag{3}
\]
The number \(399\) is an inverse of \(200\) modulo \(401\), since
\[
 200\cdot399\equiv1\pmod{401}.
\]
For purposes of taking a nonnegative representative, observe that
\[
 2^i-186-i\equiv 2^i+616-i\pmod{401},
\]
because \(616+186=802=2\cdot401\). Moreover, \(2^i+616-i\ge0\) for \(0\le i<200\). Define
\[
 Q_i=\left(399\left((2^i\bmod401)+616-i\right)\right)\bmod401
\]
for \(0\le i<200\), where the final value is chosen in \(\{0,1,\ldots,400\}\), and define
\[
 \beta_i=200Q_i+i. \tag{4}
\]
Equation (3) says precisely that
\[
 q\equiv Q_i\pmod{401}.
\]
It follows that every possible exponent satisfying (1) has the form
\[
 k=\beta_i+80200t,\qquad 0\le i<200,\quad t\ge0, \tag{5}
\]
because \(80200=200\cdot401\).

Notice also that
\[
 0\le \beta_i\le200\cdot400+199=80199<80200. \tag{6}
\]
Thus (5) is not merely a congruence: \(\beta_i\) is the canonical residue of \(k\) modulo \(80200\). In particular, if \(k<B\), then
\[
 t=\left\lfloor\frac{k}{80200}\right\rfloor.
\]
Since
\[
 B-1=16331503<204\cdot80200=16360800,
\]
we necessarily have
\[
 0\le t\le203. \tag{7}
\]
We have therefore reduced the search for a hit of \(R\) below \(B\) from more than sixteen million exponents to the finite family
\[
 \bigl\{\beta_i+80200t:0\le i<200,\ 0\le t\le203\bigr\}, \tag{8}
\]
containing \(40800\) entries before entries at or above \(B\) are discarded.

## 2. Exact modular evaluation of powers of two

We describe the modular calculation used to test the finite family (8), as well as the later covering computation.

Besides \(2^{200}\equiv1\pmod{401}\), repeated squaring gives
\[
 2^{147}\equiv1\pmod{343}.
\]
Hence
\[
 2^k\bmod401=2^{k\bmod200}\bmod401,
 \qquad
 2^k\bmod343=2^{k\bmod147}\bmod343. \tag{9}
\]
For \(k\ge2\), one also has
\[
 2^k\equiv0\pmod4. \tag{10}
\]
The three pairwise coprime moduli \(4,343,401\) have product \(N\). It is useful to give an explicit Chinese-remainder reconstruction.

Put
\[
 M=343\cdot401=137543.
\]
For integers \(b,c\) satisfying \(0\le b<343\) and \(0\le c<401\), define
\[
 x_0=\left[b+343\left(159(c+401-b)\bmod401\right)\right]\bmod M. \tag{11}
\]
Here \(343\cdot159\equiv1\pmod{401}\). It follows immediately from (11) that
\[
 x_0\equiv b\pmod{343},\qquad x_0\equiv c\pmod{401},
\]
and \(0\le x_0<M\). Now put
\[
 X(b,c)=x_0+M(x_0\bmod4). \tag{12}
\]
Since \(M=137543\equiv3\pmod4\), if \(s=x_0\bmod4\), then
\[
 X(b,c)\equiv s+3s=4s\equiv0\pmod4.
\]
Adding a multiple of \(M\) does not change the residues modulo \(343\) or \(401\). Also
\[
 0\le X(b,c)<4M=N.
\]
Thus \(X(b,c)\) is the unique representative in \([0,N-1]\) which is congruent to \(0\) modulo \(4\), to \(b\) modulo \(343\), and to \(c\) modulo \(401\).

It follows from (9), (10), and the Chinese remainder theorem that, for every \(k\ge2\),
\[
 2^k\bmod N
 =X\left(2^{k\bmod147}\bmod343,\ 2^{k\bmod200}\bmod401\right). \tag{13}
\]
For \(k=0,1\), the residues are simply computed directly. Formula (13) makes every power calculation in the finite checks below a calculation with exponents less than \(147\) or \(200\), followed by the explicit arithmetic in (11) and (12).

Finally, for any \(0\le r<N\),
\[
 2^k-k\equiv r\pmod N
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 2^k\bmod N=(r+k)\bmod N. \tag{14}
\]
Indeed, this is just the result of adding \(k\) to both sides of the congruence; because \(r\) is already the canonical residue, the statement in terms of remainders is equivalent.

## 3. The finite avoidance calculation

For each \(i=0,1,\ldots,199\), compute \(Q_i\) and \(\beta_i\) from (4). For every \(t=0,1,\ldots,203\), let
\[
 k_{i,t}=\beta_i+80200t.
\]
The following exhaustive calculation is then performed:

1. If \(k_{i,t}\ge B\), discard the pair, because it is outside the range relevant to proving absence below \(B\).
2. If \(k_{i,t}<B\), compute \(2^{k_{i,t}}\bmod N\) from (13), and compare it with
   \[
   (R+k_{i,t})\bmod N.
   \]

The outcome is as follows. The \(200\) values \(\beta_i\) are distinct, their minimum is \(66\), and their maximum is \(79123\). Among the \(40800\) pairs \((i,t)\), exactly \(81\) give \(k_{i,t}\ge B\). For each of the remaining \(40719\) pairs,
\[
 2^{k_{i,t}}\bmod N\ne(R+k_{i,t})\bmod N. \tag{15}
\]
The largest candidate below \(B\) that is tested is \(16330893\); the smallest candidate in this family at or above \(B\) is \(16331806\). These figures also provide useful boundary checks on the enumeration.

This finite calculation can equivalently be carried out by the following elementary pseudocode, which fully specifies the test:

\[
\begin{array}{l}
\text{for }i=0,\ldots,199:\\
\quad u:=2^i\bmod401;\\
\quad Q:=399\bigl((u+616-i)\bmod401\bigr)\bmod401;\\
\quad \beta:=200Q+i;\\
\quad \text{for }t=0,\ldots,203:\\
\qquad k:=\beta+80200t;\\
\qquad \text{if }k<B\text{, test (13) against }(R+k)\bmod N.
\end{array}
\]

All operations here are reductions of explicit nonnegative integers by the small moduli \(343\), \(401\), or by \(N\). Thus (15) is an exhaustive finite modular computation, not a probabilistic search.

We can now prove the desired absence statement. Suppose, for contradiction, that some \(k\) with
\[
 1\le k\le B-1
\]
satisfied \(2^k-k\equiv R\pmod N\). Section 1 would force \(k\) to equal \(k_{i,t}\) for \(i=k\bmod200<200\) and some \(t\le203\). Since \(k<B\), this pair is one of the \(40719\) tested pairs. But (15), together with equivalence (14), says it cannot hit \(R\), a contradiction. Therefore
\[
 2^k-k\not\equiv63945\pmod{550172}
 \qquad(1\le k<16331504). \tag{16}
\]

It follows immediately that no \(m<B\) gives a complete residue system: the residue \(63945\) is missing from \(f(1),\ldots,f(m)\). Hence, provided the defining minimum exists,
\[
 a(550172)\ge16331504. \tag{17}
\]
We next give a finite covering calculation that both proves existence and supplies an explicit upper bound.

## 4. A complete covering by time \(C\)

A direct finite residue sieve establishes that every residue modulo \(N\) occurs among
\[
 f(1),f(2),\ldots,f(C),
 \qquad C=17135927. \tag{18}
\]
Here is a complete description of that calculation.

Start with
\[
 y_0=1.
\]
For \(k=1,2,\ldots,C\), recursively compute
\[
 y_k=(2y_{k-1})\bmod N. \tag{19}
\]
An induction on \(k\) shows that
\[
 y_k=2^k\bmod N.
\]
At stage \(k\), mark the residue
\[
 s_k=(y_k-k)\bmod N, \tag{20}
\]
where the result is represented in \(\{0,1,\ldots,N-1\}\). By construction,
\[
 s_k\equiv2^k-k\pmod N.
\]
Maintain an array of \(N=550172\) Boolean entries, initially unmarked, and mark entry \(s_k\) at each stage. After stage \(C\), all \(550172\) entries are marked.

Equivalently, one may store for each residue \(r\) the first exponent \(K(r)\) at which it is marked and check the two inequalities and one congruence
\[
 1\le K(r)\le17135927,
 \qquad
 2^{K(r)}\bmod N=(r+K(r))\bmod N. \tag{21}
\]
Formula (13) supplies an independent short modular evaluation for every congruence in (21). The residues can be checked in blocks—for example, consecutive blocks of \(8000\) residues—without changing the mathematical content of the exhaustive check.

Some intermediate and final counts from the sieve are useful for checking its endpoints. At stage \(B-1=16331503\), exactly \(28\) residues remain unmarked. Stage \(B\) still leaves \(28\) unmarked. The last newly marked residue is
\[
 63945,
\]
and it is marked at
\[
 k=17135927=C.
\]
At that point the number of unmarked entries is zero. In particular, the finite computation proves (18).

Thus the set of positive \(m\) for which \(f(1),\ldots,f(m)\) covers every class modulo \(N\) is nonempty: it contains \(C\). Therefore its least element \(a(N)\) exists. Combining this existence with (16) proves (17). In fact, the additional endpoint information from the covering sieve shows the stronger equality \(a(N)=17135927\), but only the lower bound (17) is needed for the disproof.

## 5. Locating the \(550172\)-nd prime

It remains to relate \(B\) to the conjectured prime bound. A finite sieve of Eratosthenes up to
\[
 P=8165753
\]
gives
\[
 \pi(8165753)=550172, \tag{22}
\]
where \(\pi(x)\) denotes the number of primes at most \(x\). It also finds that \(8165753\) itself is prime. Hence
\[
 p_{550172}=8165753. \tag{23}
\]

For completeness, the primality and counting computation in (22) can be organized as follows. First list the primes up to
\[
 \lfloor\sqrt{8165753}\rfloor=2857;
\]
there are \(415\) such primes. The primality of every listed number is checked by trial division by earlier primes no larger than its square root. Then sieve the interval from \(2\) through \(8165753\), crossing out multiples of each of those \(415\) primes. A number in this interval left uncrossed is prime: if it were composite, it would have a prime divisor no larger than its square root, hence no larger than \(2857\), and would have been crossed out. Counting the uncrossed entries gives \(550172\), and the final uncrossed entry is \(8165753\). Thus (22) and (23) follow from a finite divisibility computation. The next prime is \(8165761\), although that fact is not needed.

One can use slightly less information: the count \(\pi(8165754)\ge550172\) alone implies \(p_{550172}\le8165753\), which is already sufficient because it makes the conjectured right-hand side no larger than \(B\). The exact count (22) identifies it precisely.

Finally, from (23),
\[
 2(p_{550172}-1)
 =2(8165753-1)
 =16331504
 =B. \tag{24}
\]
Together, (17) and (24) give
\[
 a(550172)\ge16331504
 =2(p_{550172}-1).
\]
Therefore
\[
 a(550172)<2(p_{550172}-1)
\]
is false. Since \(550172>0\), this is a counterexample to the conjecture that the strict inequality holds for every positive \(n\).
